newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police break up opposition rallies.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police break up opposition rallies.

text.p: Police used batons to sweep anti-government protesters off the streets in two Albanian cities on Saturday, but popular discontent over bankrupt pyramid investment schemes showed no sign of subsiding.
Riot police beat demonstrators and reporters in the capital Tirana and the southern town of Fier and briefly detained leaders of the opposition Socialist party.

But security forces stayed clear of tens of thousands of people who massed for the fourth consecutive day in the Adriatic port of Vlore. Crowds chanted slogans against President Sali Berisha and demanded their lost savings back.

An alliance of 10 opposition parties, in the Forum for Democracy, called a rally for Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square to press for the resignation of the rightist government which it holds responsible for the demise of the pyramid funds.
The interior ministry banned the protest, saying it posed a security threat, and police sealed off the heart of the city.
When around 500 marchers tried to reach the huge central square, riot police moved in, lashing out with their batons and bundling three Socialist Party leaders into a security car.

"I was hit 10, 15 times and three men in plain clothes took put me into a car where I was beaten some more," prominent Socialist Kastriot Islami, a large violet welt on his forehead, told Reuters. He was held at a police station for two hours.
"We have to keep trying to establish dialogue. We will try to organise peaceful protests," he added. Opposition officials said 15 of their leaders were detained but later released.
Police also targeted reporters trying to cover the rally.
Three men identifying themselves as members of "special security forces" entered Reuters Tirana bureau and demanded pictures and television film before being asked to leave.
Around 400 supporters of the ruling Democratic Party held a counter demonstration close to Skanderbeg square, in the shadow of a new party headquarters under construction.
Police did not intervene. Nor did they prevent a convoy of cars racing around the dusty city centre, horns blaring and Democratic Party flags fluttering from the windows.

Locals believe more than $2 billion might be tied up in Albania's get-rich-quick pyramids. Some of the schemes are still limping on, but the recent collapse of five large funds has left hundreds of thousands of people facing economic ruin.

The crisis sparked widespread disturbances in January but the unrest was capped after a wave of nationwide arrests and the government started handing out partial refunds to investors from two failed schemes last week.
However fresh protests erupted in Vlore last week after a locally based fund, which owed some $500 million, caved in.
Police initially tried to break up the Vlore rallies, but were overwhelmed by the sheer number of protesters.
Locals in nearby Fier also tried to demonstrate on Saturday, but their rally was immediately suppressed.
Reuters correspondent Benet Koleka was beaten and police seized his notebook. Associated Press' photographer and cameraman were punched and had some of their equipment taken.
Smaller protests have also burst out in other parts of volatile southern Albania, with protesters in the town of Memaliaj blocking the main road south to Greece for the second day in a row.
The Democratic Party has accused the Socialists of taking advantage of the crisis and seeking to seize power.

The Democrats won re-election last year in polls criticised as unfair by Western observers. Some opposition politicians accuse the party of financing the victory with proceeds from the failed pyramid companies.
